text.p: Momentarily ignoring questions about his political fate, House Speaker Newt Gingrich said Monday Congress and President Clinton could be on the verge of forging a new coalition bent on balanced budgets, lower taxes and welfare reform.

The Georgia Republican told a packed Chamber of Commerce breakfast meeting that the 104th Congress won its "core argument" about political priorities when Clinton signed the welfare bill into law last year. "That's certainly an act of broadly being inside the same coalition we're in," Gingrich said.
With the 105th Congress set to convene Tuesday, he predicted more progress towards a balanced budget, lower capital gains tax, tax breaks for education and tougher measures to combat drug use.

"There is now virtually universal agreement -- not total -- but virtually universal agreement that we are working to balance the budget by 2002, that that is a bipartisan effort and that it will be a budget balanced with lower taxes," Gingrich said.
"The president basically broadly agrees," he said. "We're arguing about details ... but the direction is the same."

A year ago, Gingrich charged into a budget showdown with Clinton that wound up with the government shutting down twice and in the end cost Gingrich and his fellow Republicans dearly as voters last November reduced the party's majority in the House.
But Gingrich said House Republicans now were looking forward to working in concert with moderate Democrats.

"I'm not sure who the other side is right now. I know who my opponents are because they're on TV every Sunday," he said, in a quip about debates on Sunday talk shows about whether he should step aside as speaker.
"I think we're at the edge here of potentially a brand new large coalition that is really able to bring people in from all backgrounds," he added, turning back to the policy question.

His hour-long speech was his first public appearance since he admitted to House ethics violations two weeks ago. His message centred on the need for cooperation in helping America reach its economic, political and social potential in the new century.
He later boarded a plane bound for Washington, where he was scheduled to meet Republicans in a closed-door session that could determine whether he will be re-elected Tuesday.
"As all of you can imagine, the last month has been relatively difficult. It is not something I would ever voluntarily suggest to anyone," Gingrich said.

"On the other hand, it is the way a great nation tries to lead itself. This is a hard and difficult business and the fact is that we are making progress. And we're going to continue to make progress."
